listen_text: Section. Introduction. In chapter Steps towards set theory Z , we postulated that there is an infinite-th stage of the hierarchy, in the form of Stages hit infinity (see also our axiom of Infinity). However, given Stages keep going, we can't stop at the infinite-th stage; we have to keep going. So: at the next stage after the first infinite stage, we form all possible collections of sets that were available at the first infinite stage; and repeat; and repeat; and repeat; and so on Implicitly what has happened here is that we have started to invoke an “intuitive” notion of number, according to which there can be numbers after all the natural numbers. In particular, the notion involved is that of a transfinite ordinal. The aim of this chapter is to make this idea more rigorous. We will explore the general notion of an ordinal, and then explicitly define certain sets to be our ordinals. End section.

A well-ordering is a pair the ordered pair consisting of capital A and the less-than relation , such that is less than well-orders capital A . In this case, we write capital A under less-than is order-isomorphic to capital B under less-dot , and say that f is an order-isomorphism. End definition. In what follows, for brevity, we will speak of “isomorphisms” rather than “order-isomorphisms”. Intuitively, isomorphisms are structure-preserving bijections. Compositions of isomorphisms are isomorphisms, that is: if f maps capital A to capital B and g maps capital B to capital C are isomorphisms, then g composed with f maps capital A to capital C is an isomorphism. End proposition. Proof. Let f and g be isomorphisms functions from capital A to capital B . We will prove the result by induction, that is using proposition two in chapter Ordinals . Fix a belongs to capital A , and suppose (for induction) that for every b less than a, f of b equals g of b . Fix x belongs to capital B . listen_text: Section. Basic Properties of the Ordinals. We observed that the first few ordinals are the natural numbers. The main reason for developing a theory of ordinals is to extend the principle of induction which holds on the natural numbers. We will build up to this via a sequence of elementary results. Lemma. Every element of an ordinal is an ordinal. End lemma. Proof. Let alpha be an ordinal with b belongs to alpha . Since alpha is transitive, b is a subset of alpha . So the membership relation well-orders b as the membership relation well-orders alpha . To see that b is transitive, suppose x belongs to c, and c belongs to b . So c belongs to alpha as b is a subset of alpha . Again, as alpha is transitive, c is a subset of alpha , so that x belongs to alpha . So x, c, and b belong to alpha . But the membership relation well-orders alpha , so that the membership relation is a transitive relation on alpha by proposition one in chapter Ordinals . So since x belongs to c, and c belongs to b , we have x belongs to b . Generalising, c is a subset of b End proof. Corollary. alpha equals the set of ordinals beta that belong to alpha , for any ordinal alpha End corollary. Proof. Immediate from lemma five in chapter Ordinals . End proof. The rough gist of the next two main results, theorem Transfinite Induction in chapter Ordinals and theorem Trichotomy in chapter Ordinals , is that the ordinals themselves are well-ordered by membership: Theorem. Transfinite Induction. For any formula phi of x : Displayed expression. if some alpha satisfies phi, then there is an alpha satisfying phi such that no beta belonging to alpha satisfies phi. End displayed expression. where the displayed quantifiers are implicitly restricted to ordinals. End theorem. Proof. Suppose phi of alpha , for some ordinal alpha . If for every beta in alpha, not phi of beta , then we are done. Otherwise, as alpha is an ordinal, it has some the membership relation -least element which is phi , and this is an ordinal by lemma five in chapter Ordinals . End proof. Note that we can equally express theorem Transfinite Induction in chapter Ordinals as the scheme: Displayed expression. if phi holds of every alpha whenever it holds of every beta belonging to alpha, then phi holds of every alpha. End displayed expression. just by taking not phi of alpha in theorem Transfinite Induction in chapter Ordinals , and then performing elementary logical manipulations. Theorem. Trichotomy. alpha belongs to beta or alpha equals beta or beta belongs to alpha , for any ordinals alpha and beta . End theorem. Proof. The proof is by double induction, that is, using theorem Transfinite Induction in chapter Ordinals twice. Say that x is comparable with y if and only if x belongs to y or x equals y or y belongs to x . For induction, suppose that every ordinal in alpha is comparable with every ordinal. For further induction, suppose that alpha is comparable with every ordinal in beta . We will show that alpha is comparable with beta . By induction on beta , it will follow that alpha is comparable with every ordinal; and so by induction on alpha , every ordinal is comparable with every ordinal, as required. It suffices to assume that alpha does not belong to beta and beta does not belong to alpha , and show that alpha equals beta . To show that alpha is a subset of beta , fix gamma belongs to alpha ; this is an ordinal by lemma five in chapter Ordinals . So by the first induction hypothesis, gamma is comparable with beta . But if either gamma equals beta or beta belongs to gamma then beta belongs to alpha (invoking the fact that alpha is transitive if necessary), contrary to our assumption; so gamma belongs to beta . Generalising, alpha is a subset of beta . Exactly similar reasoning, using the second induction hypothesis, shows that beta is a subset of alpha . So alpha equals beta . End proof. As such, we will sometimes write alpha is less than beta rather than alpha belongs to beta , since the membership relation is behaving as an ordering relation. There are no deep reasons for this, beyond familiarity, and because it is easier to write alpha is less than or equal to beta than alpha belongs to beta or alpha equals beta . Footnote. We could write alpha bears the underlined membership relation to beta ; but that would be wholly non-standard. End footnote. Here are two quick consequences of our last results, the first of which puts our new notation into action: Corollary. If there exists alpha, phi of alpha , then there exists an alpha satisfying phi such that every beta satisfying phi is greater than or equal to alpha . Moreover, for any ordinals alpha, then beta, then gamma , both alpha does not belong to alpha and if alpha belongs to beta and beta belongs to gamma, then alpha belongs to gamma . End corollary. Proof. Just like proposition one in chapter Ordinals . End proof. Exercise. Complete the “exactly similar reasoning” in the proof of theorem Trichotomy in chapter Ordinals . End exercise. This exercise remains unsolved. Corollary. capital A is an ordinal if and only if capital A is a transitive set of ordinals. End corollary. Proof. Left-to-right. By lemma five in chapter Ordinals . Right-to-left. If capital A is a transitive set of ordinals, then the membership relation well-orders capital A by theorem Transfinite Induction in chapter Ordinals and theorem Trichotomy in chapter Ordinals . End proof. Now, we glossed theorem Transfinite Induction in chapter Ordinals and theorem Trichotomy in chapter Ordinals as telling us that the membership relation well-orders the ordinals. However, we have to be very cautious about this sort of claim, thanks to the following result: Theorem. Burali-Forti Paradox. There is no set of all the ordinals End theorem. Proof. For reductio, suppose capital O is the set of all ordinals. If alpha belongs to beta, and beta belongs to capital O , then alpha is an ordinal, by lemma five in chapter Ordinals , so alpha belongs to capital O . So capital O is transitive, and hence capital O is an ordinal by corollary four in chapter Ordinals . Hence capital O belongs to capital O , contradicting corollary three in chapter Ordinals . End proof. This result is named after Cesare Burali-Forti . But, it was Cantor in one thousand eight hundred ninety nine—in a letter to Dedekind—who first saw clearly the contradiction in supposing that there is a set of all the ordinals. As van Heijenoort explains: Quotation. Burali-Forti himself considered the contradiction as establishing, by reductio ad absurdum, the result that the natural ordering of the ordinals is just a partial ordering. And if alpha equals beta , then alpha is a subset of beta and beta is a subset of alpha . So by theorem Trichotomy in chapter Ordinals we are done. End proof. Proposition. alpha equals beta if and only if alpha is order-isomorphic to beta , for any ordinals alpha, then beta . End proposition. Proof. listen_text: Section. Replacement. In section Von Neumann's Construction of the Ordinals in chapter Ordinals , we motivated the introduction of ordinals by suggesting that we could treat them as order-types, that is, canonical proxies for well-orderings. In order for that to work, we would need to prove that every well-ordering is isomorphic to some ordinal. This would allow us to define the order type of capital A under the less-than relation as the ordinal alpha such that capital A under less-than is isomorphic to alpha . Unfortunately, we cannot prove the desired result only the Axioms we provided introduced so far. (We will see why in section The Strength of Replacement in chapter Replacement , but for now the point is: we can't.) We need a new thought, and here it is: Axiom. Scheme of Replacement. For any formula phi of x and y , the following is an axiom: Quotation. for any capital A , if for every x in capital A, there exists exactly one y, phi of x and y , then the set of y such that there exists x in capital A, phi of x and y exists. End quotation. End axiom. As with Separation, this is a scheme: it yields infinitely many axioms, for each of the infinitely many different phi apostrophe s . And it can equally well be (and normally is) written down thus: For any formula phi of x and y which does not contain “ capital B ”, the following is an axiom: Displayed expression. for every capital A, if every x in capital A has exactly one y such that phi holds of x and y, then there exists a capital B such that, for every y, y belongs to capital B if and only if phi holds of x and y for some x in capital A. End displayed expression. On first encounter, however, this is quite a tangled formula. The following quick consequence of Replacement probably gives a clearer expression to the intuitive idea we are working with: Footnote. A term is an expression which picks out exactly one object (on any completion of its free variables). For example, “ the empty set ” is a term which picks out the empty set; “ the set containing x ” is a term which picks out x apostrophe s singleton (whatever x might be); “ x union y ” is a term which picks out the union of x and y (whatever they might be). End footnote. Corollary. For any term tau of x , and any set capital A , this set exists: Displayed expression. the set of tau of x such that x belongs to capital A, equals the set of y such that there exists x in capital A, y equals tau of x. End displayed expression. End corollary. Proof. Since tau is a term, for every x, there exists exactly one y, tau of x equals y . A fortiori, for every x in capital A, there exists exactly one y, tau of x equals y . So the set of y such that there exists x in capital A, tau of x equals y exists by Replacement. End proof. This suggests that “Replacement” is a good name for the Axiom: given a set capital A , you can form a new set, the set of tau of x such that x belongs to capital A , by replacing every member of capital A with its image under tau . Indeed, following the notation for the image of a set under a function, we might write the image of capital A under tau for the set of tau of x such that x belongs to capital A . Crucially, however, tau is a term. It need not be (a name for) a function, in the sense of section Functions as Relations in chapter Functions , that is, a certain set of ordered pairs. After all, if f is a function (in that sense), then the set the image of capital A under f equals the set of f of x such that x belongs to capital A is just a particular subset of the range of f , and that is already guaranteed to exist, just using the axioms of set theory Z minus . Footnote. Just consider the set of y in the double union of f such that y equals f of x for some x in capital A . End footnote. Replacement, by contrast, is a powerful addition to our axioms, as we will see in chapter Replacement . End section.

The theory set theory Z F minus has these axioms: Extensionality, Union, Pairs, Powersets, Infinity, and all instances of the Separation and Replacement schemes. Otherwise put, set theory Z F minus adds Replacement to set theory Z minus . End definition. This stands for Zermelo—Fraenkel set theory ( minus something which we will come to later). End section.

listen_text: Section. Successor and Limit Ordinals. In the next few chapters, we will use ordinals a great deal. So it will help if we introduce some simple notions. Definition. For any ordinal alpha , its successor is the ordinal successor of alpha equals alpha union the set containing alpha . We say that alpha is a successor ordinal if the ordinal successor of beta equals alpha for some ordinal beta . We say that alpha is a limit ordinal if and only if alpha is neither empty nor a successor ordinal. End definition. The following result shows that this is the right notion of successor: Proposition. For any ordinal alpha : List. Next item. alpha belongs to the ordinal successor of alpha ; Next item. the ordinal successor of alpha is an ordinal; Next item. there is no ordinal beta such that alpha belongs to beta, and beta belongs to the ordinal successor of alpha . End list. End proposition. Proof. Trivially, alpha belongs to alpha union the set containing alpha equals the ordinal successor of alpha . Equally, the ordinal successor of alpha is a transitive set of ordinals, and hence an ordinal by corollary four in chapter Ordinals . And it is impossible that alpha belongs to beta, and beta belongs to the ordinal successor of alpha , since then either beta belongs to alpha or beta equals alpha , contradicting corollary three in chapter Ordinals . End proof. This also licenses a variant of proof by transfinite induction: Theorem. Simple Transfinite Induction. Let phi of x be a formula such that: List. Next item. phi of the empty set ; and Next item. for any ordinal alpha , if phi of alpha then phi of the ordinal successor of alpha ; and Next item. if alpha is a limit ordinal and for every beta in alpha, phi of beta , then phi of alpha . End list. Then for every alpha, phi of alpha . End theorem. Proof. We prove the contrapositive. So, suppose there is some ordinal which is not phi ; let gamma be the least such ordinal. Then either gamma equals the empty set , or gamma equals the ordinal successor of alpha for some alpha such that phi of alpha ; or gamma is a limit ordinal and for every beta in gamma, phi of beta . End proof. A final bit of notation will prove helpful later on: Definition. If capital X is a set of ordinals, then the strict supremum of capital X equals the union, over alpha in capital X, of the ordinal successors of alpha . End definition. Here, “lsub” stands for “least strict upper bound”. Footnote. Some books use “ the supremum of capital X ” for this. But other books use “ the supremum of capital X ” for the least non-strict upper bound, that is, simply the union of capital X . If capital X has a greatest element, alpha , these notions come apart: the least strict upper bound is the ordinal successor of alpha , whereas the least non-strict upper bound is just alpha . End footnote. The following result explains this: Proposition. If capital X is a set of ordinals, the strict supremum of capital X is the least ordinal greater than every ordinal in capital X . End proposition. Proof. Let capital Y equals the set of ordinal successors of alpha as alpha ranges over capital X , so that the strict supremum of capital X equals the union of capital Y . Since ordinals are transitive and every member of an ordinal is an ordinal, the strict supremum of capital X is a transitive set of ordinals, and so is an ordinal by corollary four in chapter Ordinals . If alpha belongs to capital X , then the ordinal successor of alpha belongs to capital Y , so the ordinal successor of alpha is a subset of the union of capital Y equals the strict supremum of capital X , and hence alpha belongs to the strict supremum of capital X . So the strict supremum of capital X is strictly greater than every ordinal in capital X . Conversely, if alpha belongs to the strict supremum of capital X , then alpha belongs to the ordinal successor of beta, and that successor belongs to capital Y for some beta belongs to capital X , so that alpha is less than or equal to beta, and beta belongs to capital X . So the strict supremum of capital X is the least strict upper bound on capital X . End proof. End section. End chapter.

listen_text: Section. Foundation. We are only almost done—and not quite finished—because nothing in set theory Z F minus guarantees that every set is in some capital V subscript alpha , that is, that every set is formed at some stage. Now, there is a fairly straightforward (mathematical) sense in which we don't care whether there are sets outside the hierarchy. (If there are any there, we can simply ignore them.) But we have motivated our concept of set with the thought that every set is formed at some stage (see Stages are key in section The Story in More Detail in chapter Steps towards set theory Z ). So we will want to preclude the possibility of sets which fall outside of the hierarchy. Accordingly, we must add a new axiom, which ensures that every set occurs somewhere in the hierarchy. Since the capital V subscript alpha s are our stages, we might simply consider adding the following as an axiom: Regularity. for every capital A, there exists alpha, capital A is a subset of capital V subscript alpha This would be a perfectly reasonable approach. However, for reasons that will be explained in the next section, we will instead adopt an alternative axiom: Axiom. Foundation. for every capital A not equal to the empty set, there exists capital B in capital A, capital A intersected with capital B equals the empty set . End axiom. We are only almost done—and not quite finished—because nothing in set theory Z F minus guarantees that every set is in some capital V subscript alpha , that is, that every set is formed at some stage. listen_text: Section. set theory Z and set theory Z F : A Milestone. With Foundation, we reach another important milestone. We have considered theories set theory Z minus and set theory Z F minus , which we said were certain theories “minus” a certain something. That certain something is Foundation. So: Definition. The theory set theory Z adds Foundation to set theory Z minus . So its axioms are Extensionality, Union, Pairs, Powersets, Infinity, Foundation, and all instances of the Separation scheme. The theory set theory Z F adds Foundation to set theory Z F minus . Otherwise put, set theory Z F adds all instances of Replacement to set theory Z . End definition. Still, one question might have occurred to you. If Regularity is equivalent over set theory Z F minus to Foundation, and Regularity's justification is clear, why bother to go around the houses, and take Foundation as our basic axiom, rather than Regularity? Setting aside historical reasons (to do with who formulated what and when), the basic reason is that Foundation can be presented without employing the definition of the capital V subscript alpha s. That definition relied upon all of the work of section The Transfinite Recursion Theorem(s) in chapter Stages and Ranks : we needed to prove Transfinite Recursion, to show that it was justified. But our proof of Transfinite Recursion employed Replacement. So, whilst Foundation and Regularity are equivalent modulo set theory Z F minus , they are not equivalent modulo set theory Z minus . Indeed, the matter is more drastic than this simple remark suggests. Though it goes well beyond this book's remit, it turns out that both set theory Z minus and set theory Z are too weak to define the capital V subscript alpha s. So, if you are working only in set theory Z , then Regularity (as we have formulated it) does not even make sense. This is why our official axiom is Foundation, rather than Regularity. From now on, we will work in set theory Z F (unless otherwise stated), without any further comment. End section.

listen_text: Section. Introduction. Replacement is the axiom scheme which makes the difference between set theory Z F and set theory Z . We helped ourselves to it throughout chapters Ordinals through Stages and Ranks . In this chapter, we will finally consider the question: is Replacement justified? To make the question sharp, it is worth observing that Replacement is really rather strong. We will get a sense of just how strong it is, during this chapter (and again in section aleph-Fixed Points in chapter Cardinal Arithmetic ). But this will suggest that justification really is required. We will discuss two kinds of justification. Roughly: an extrinsic justification is an attempt to justify an axiom by its fruits; an intrinsic justification is an attempt to justify an axiom by suggesting that it is vindicated by the mathematical concepts in question. We will get a greater sense of what this means during this chapter, but it is just the tip of an iceberg. For more, see in particular Penelope Maddy ( one thousand nine hundred eighty eight and one thousand nine hundred eighty eight ). End section.

listen_text: Section. The Strength of Replacement. We begin with a simple observation about the strength of Replacement: unless we go beyond set theory Z , we cannot prove the existence of any von Neumann ordinal greater than or equal to omega plus omega . Here is a sketch of why. Working in set theory Z F , consider the set capital V subscript omega plus omega . This set acts as the domain for a model for set theory Z . To see this, we introduce some notation for the relativization of a formula: Definition. For any set capital M , and any formula phi , let phi superscript capital M be the formula which results by restricting all of phi apostrophe s quantifiers to capital M . That is, replace “ there exists x ” with “ open scope, there exists x belongs to capital M, close scope ”, and replace “ for every x ” with “ open scope, for every x belongs to capital M, close scope ”. End definition. It can be shown that, for every axiom phi of set theory Z , we have that set theory Z F derives phi superscript capital V subscript omega plus omega . But omega plus omega is not in capital V subscript omega plus omega , by corollary two in chapter Stages and Ranks . So set theory Z is consistent with the non-existence of omega plus omega . This is why we said, in section Replacement in chapter Ordinals , that theorem five in chapter Ordinals cannot be proved without Replacement. For it is easy, within set theory Z , to define an explicit well-ordering which intuitively should have order-type omega plus omega . Indeed, we gave an informal example of this in section The General Idea of an Ordinal in chapter Ordinals , when we presented the ordering on the natural numbers given by: Displayed expression. Source-ordered display. n is strictly smaller than m if and only if either, n is less than m and m minus n, is even,. Then, or n is even and m is odd.. End display. End displayed expression. But if omega plus omega does not exist, this well-ordering is not isomorphic to any ordinal. So set theory Z does not prove theorem five in chapter Ordinals . Flipping things around: Replacement allows us to prove the existence of omega plus omega , and hence must allow us to prove the existence of capital V subscript omega plus omega . And not just that. For any well-ordering we can define, theorem five in chapter Ordinals tells us that there is some alpha isomorphic with that well-ordering, and hence that capital V subscript alpha exists. In a straightforward way, then, Replacement guarantees that the hierarchy of sets must be very tall. Over the next few sections, and then again in section aleph-Fixed Points in chapter Cardinal Arithmetic , we'll get a better sense of better just how tall Replacement forces the hierarchy to be. The simple point, for now, is that Replacement really does stand in need of justification! End section.

listen_text: Section. Limitation-of-size. Perhaps the most common attempt to offer an “intrinsic” justification of Replacement comes via the following notion: List. Next item.. Limitation of size. Any things form a set, provided that there are not too many of them. End list. This principle will immediately vindicate Replacement. After all, any set formed by Replacement cannot be any larger than any set from which it was formed. Stated precisely: suppose you form a set the image of capital A under tau equals the set of tau of x such that x belongs to capital A using Replacement; then the image of capital A under tau has cardinality at most that of capital A ; so if the elements of capital A were not too numerous to form a set, their images are not too numerous to form the image of capital A under tau . The obvious difficulty with invoking Limitation of size to justify Replacement is that we have not yet laid down any principle like Limitation of size. Moreover, when we told our story about the cumulative-iterative conception of set in chapters The Iterative Conception through Steps towards set theory Z , nothing ever hinted in the direction of Limitation of size. This, indeed, is precisely why Boolos at one point wrote: “Perhaps one may conclude that there are at least two thoughts `behind' set theory” (one thousand nine hundred eighty nine, page nineteen) . On the one hand, the ideas surrounding the cumulative-iterative conception of set are meant to vindicate set theory Z . On the other hand, Limitation of size is meant to vindicate Replacement. But the issue it is not just that we have thus far been silent about Limitation of size. Rather, the issue is that Limitation of size (as just formulated) seems to sit quite badly with the cumulative-iterative notion of set. After all, it mentions nothing about the idea of sets as formed in stages. This is really not much of a surprise, given the history of these “two thoughts” (that is, the cumulative-iterative conception of set, and Limitation of size ). These “two thoughts” ultimately amount to two rather different projects for blocking the set-theoretic paradoxes. The cumulative-iterative notion of set blocks Russell's paradox by saying, roughly: we should never have expected a Russell set to exist, because it would not be “formed” at any stage. By contrast, Limitation of size is meant to rule out the Russell set, by saying, roughly: we should never have expected a Russell set to exist, because it would have been too big. Put like this, then, let's be blunt: considered as a reply to the paradoxes, Limitation of size stands in need of much more justification. Consider, for example, this version of Russell's Paradox: no pug sniffs exactly the pugs which don't sniff themselves (see section Russell's Paradox (again) in chapter The Iterative Conception ). If you ask “why is there no such pug?”, it is not a good answer to be told that such a pug would have to sniff too many pugs. So why would it be a good intuitive explanation, of the non-existence of a Russell set, that it would have to be “too big” to exist? In short, it's forgivable if you are a bit mystified concerning the “intuitive” motivation for Limitation of size. End section.

listen_text: Section. Replacement and “Absolute Infinity”. We will now put Limitation of size behind us, and explore a different family of (intrinsic) attempts to justify Replacement, which do take seriously the idea of the sets as formed in stages. When we first outlined the iterative process, we offered some principles which explained what happens at each stage. These were Stages are key, Stages are ordered, and Stages accumulate. Later, we added some principles which told us something about the number of stages: Stages keep going told us that the process of set-formation never ends, and Stages hit infinity told us that the process goes through an infinite-th stage. It is reasonable to suggest that these two latter principles fall out of some a broader principle, like: List. Next item.. Stages are inexhaustible. There are absolutely infinitely many stages; the hierarchy is as tall as it could possibly be. End list. Obviously this is an informal principle. But even if it is not immediately entailed by the cumulative-iterative conception of set, it certainly seems consonant with it. At the very least, and unlike Limitation of size, it retains the idea that sets are formed stage-by-stage. The hope, now, is to leverage Stages are inexhaustible into a justification of Replacement. So let us see how this might be done. In section The General Idea of an Ordinal in chapter Ordinals , we saw that it is easy to construct a well-ordering which (morally) should be isomorphic to omega plus omega . Otherwise put, we can easily imagine a stage-by-stage iterative process, whose order-type (morally) is omega plus omega . As such, if we have accepted Stages are inexhaustible, then we should surely accept that there is at least an omega plus omega indexed stage of the hierarchy, that is, capital V subscript omega plus omega , for the hierarchy surely could continue thus far. This thought generalizes as follows: for any well-ordering, the process of building the iterative hierarchy should run at least as far as that well-ordering. And we could guarantee this, just by treating theorem five in chapter Ordinals as an axiom. This would tell us that any well-ordering is isomorphic to a von Neumann ordinal. Since each von Neumann ordinal will be equal to its own rank, theorem five in chapter Ordinals will then tell us that, whenever we can describe a well-ordering in our set theory, the iterative process of set building must outrun that well-ordering. This idea certainly seems like a corollary of Stages are inexhaustible. Unfortunately, if our aim is to extract Replacement from this idea, then we face a simple, technical, barrier: Replacement is strictly stronger than theorem five in chapter Ordinals . (This observation is made by Michael Potter (two thousand four), section thirteen point two ; we will prove it in section Appendix: Finite axiomatizability in chapter Replacement .) The upshot is that, if we are going to understand Stages are inexhaustible in such a way as to yield Replacement, then it cannot merely say that the hierarchy outruns any well-ordering. It must make a stronger claim than that. To this end, Joseph R. Shoenfield (one thousand nine hundred seventy seven) proposed a very natural strengthening of the idea, as follows: the hierarchy is not cofinal with any set. Footnote. Gödel seems to have proposed a similar thought; see Michael Potter (two thousand four), page two hundred twenty three . For discussion of Gödel and Joseph R. Shoenfield , see Luca Incurvati (two thousand twenty), ninety through ninety five . End footnote. In slightly more detail: if tau is a mapping which sends sets to stages of the hierarchy, the image of any set capital A under tau does not exhaust the hierarchy. Otherwise put (schematically): List. Next item.. Stages are super cofinal. If capital A is a set and tau of x is a stage for every x belongs to capital A , then there is a stage which comes after each tau of x for x belongs to capital A . End list. It is obvious that set theory Z F proves a suitably formalised version of Stages are super cofinal. Conversely, we can informally argue that Stages are super cofinal justifies Replacement. Footnote. It would be harder to prove Replacement using some formalisation of Stages are super cofinal, since set theory Z on its own is not strong enough to define the stages, so it is not clear how one would formalise Stages are super cofinal. One option, though, is to work in some extension of the language of set theory , as discussed in section Extrinsic Considerations about Replacement in chapter Replacement . End footnote. For suppose for every x in capital A, there exists exactly one y, phi of x and y . Then for each x belongs to capital A , let sigma of x be the y such that phi of x and y , and let tau of x be the stage at which sigma of x is first formed. By Stages are super cofinal, there is a stage capital V such that for every x in capital A, tau of x belongs to capital V . Now since each tau of x belongs to capital V and sigma of x is a subset of tau of x , by Separation we can obtain the set of y belongs to capital V such that there exists x in capital A, sigma of x equals y, equals the set of y such that there exists x in capital A, phi of x and y . Exercise. Formalize Stages are super cofinal within set theory Z F . End exercise. This exercise remains unsolved. So Stages are super cofinal vindicates Replacement. And it is at least plausible that Stages are inexhaustible vindicates Stages are super cofinal. For suppose Stages are super cofinal fails. So the hierarchy is cofinal with some set capital A , that is, we have a map tau such that for any stage capital S there is some x belongs to capital A such that capital S belongs to tau of x . In that case, we do have a way to get a handle on the supposed “absolute infinity” of the hierarchy: it is exhausted by the range of tau applied to capital A . And that compromises the thought that the hierarchy is “absolutely infinite”. Contraposing: Stages are inexhaustible entails Stages are super cofinal, which in turn justifies Replacement. This represents a genuinely promising attempt to provide an intrinsic justification for Replacement. But whether it ultimately works, or not, we will have to leave to you to decide. End section.

listen_text: Section. Replacement and Reflection. Our last attempt to justify Replacement, via Stages are inexhaustible, begins with a deep and lovely result: Footnote. A reminder: all formulas can have parameters (unless explicitly stated otherwise). End footnote. Theorem. Reflection Schema. For any formula phi : Displayed expression. for every ordinal alpha there exists an ordinal beta greater than alpha such that, for all x subscript one through x subscript n in capital V subscript beta, phi holds of those objects if and only if its relativization to capital V subscript beta holds of them. End displayed expression. End theorem. As in definition one in chapter Replacement , phi superscript capital V subscript beta is the result of restricting every quantifier in phi to the set capital V subscript beta . So, intuitively, Reflection says this: if phi is true in the entire hierarchy, then phi is true in arbitrarily many initial segments of the hierarchy. Richard Montague (one thousand nine hundred sixty one) and Azriel Lévy (one thousand nine hundred sixty) showed that (suitable formulations of) Replacement and Reflection are equivalent, modulo set theory Z , so that adding either gives you set theory Z F . (We prove these results in section Appendix: Results surrounding Replacement in chapter Replacement .) Given this equivalence, one might hope to justify Reflection and Replacement via Stages are inexhaustible as follows: given Stages are inexhaustible, the hierarchy should be very, very tall; so tall, in fact, that nothing we can say about it is sufficient to bound its height. And we can understand this as the thought that, if any sentence phi is true in the entire hierarchy, then it is true in arbitrarily many initial segments of the hierarchy. And that is just Reflection. Again, this seems like a genuinely promising attempt to provide an intrinsic justification for Replacement. But there is much too much to say about it here. You must now decide for yourself whether it succeeds. Footnote. Though you might like to continue by reading Luca Incurvati (two thousand twenty), ninety five through one hundred . End footnote. End section.

listen_text: Section. Appendix: Finite axiomatizability. We close this chapter by extracting some results from Replacement. The first result is due to Richard Montague (one thousand nine hundred sixty one) ; note that it is not a proof within set theory Z F , but a proof about set theory Z F : Theorem. set theory Z F is not finitely axiomatizable. More generally: if the theory of capital T is finite and the theory of capital T set theory Z F is derivable , then the theory of capital T is inconsistent. (Here, we tacitly restrict ourselves to first-order sentences whose only non-logical primitive is the membership relation , and we write the theory of capital T set theory Z F is derivable to indicate that the theory of capital T phi is derivable for all phi belongs to set theory Z F .) End theorem. Proof. Fix finite the theory of capital T such that the theory of capital T set theory Z F is derivable . So, the theory of capital T proves Reflection, that is theorem Reflection Schema in chapter Replacement . Since the theory of capital T is finite, we can rewrite it as a single conjunction, theta . Reflecting with this formula, the theory of capital T there exists beta, open scope, theta if and only if theta superscript capital V subscript beta, close scope is derivable . Since trivially the theory of capital T theta is derivable , we find that the theory of capital T there exists beta, theta superscript capital V subscript beta is derivable . Now, let psi of capital X abbreviate: Displayed expression. theta superscript capital X and capital X, is transitive and for every capital Y in capital X, open scope, capital Y, is transitive implies not theta superscript capital Y, close scope. End displayed expression. roughly this says: capital X is a transitive model of theta , and the membership relation -minimal in this regard. Now, recalling that the theory of capital T there exists beta, theta superscript capital V subscript beta is derivable , by basic facts about ranks within set theory Z F and hence within the theory of capital T , we have: Displayed expression. the theory of capital T there exists capital M, psi of capital M applied to tag applied to star is derivable. End displayed expression. Using the first conjunct of psi of capital X , whenever the theory of capital T sigma is derivable , we have that the theory of capital T for every capital X, open scope, psi of capital X implies sigma superscript capital X, close scope is derivable . So, by equation star in chapter Replacement : Displayed expression. source-ordered derivation in theory capital T. First, capital T derives that every capital X satisfying psi also satisfies, inside capital X, that some capital N satisfies psi. Using this and equation star in chapter Replacement, capital T derives a capital M satisfying psi in which some capital N satisfies psi. In particular, capital T derives such a capital M containing a capital N that is internally transitive and satisfies theta through the displayed relativizations. Finally, by transitivity, capital T derives a capital M satisfying psi that contains a transitive capital N satisfying theta. End derivation. End displayed expression. So that the theory of capital T is inconsistent. Footnote. This “elementary reasoning” involves proving certain “absoluteness facts” for transitive sets. End footnote. End proof. Here is a similar result, noted by Michael Potter (two thousand four), two hundred twenty three : Proposition. Let the theory of capital T extend set theory Z with finitely many new axioms. If the theory of capital T set theory Z F is derivable , then the theory of capital T is inconsistent. (Here we use the same tacit restrictions as for theorem three in chapter Replacement .) End proposition. Proof. Use theta for the conjunction of all of the theory of capital T apostrophe s axioms except for the (infinitely many) instances of Separation. Defining psi from theta as in theorem three in chapter Replacement , we can show that the theory of capital T there exists capital M, psi of capital M is derivable . As in theorem three in chapter Replacement , we can establish the schema that, whenever the theory of capital T sigma is derivable , we have that the theory of capital T for every capital X, open scope, psi of capital X implies sigma superscript capital X, close scope is derivable . We then finish our proof, exactly as in theorem three in chapter Replacement . However, establishing the schema involves a little more work than in theorem three in chapter Replacement . After all, the Separation-instances are in the theory of capital T , but they are not conjuncts of theta . However, we can overcome this obstacle by proving that the theory of capital T for every capital X, open scope, capital X, is transitive implies sigma superscript capital X, close scope is derivable , for every Separation-instance sigma . We leave this to the reader. End proof. Exercise. Show that, for every Separation-instance sigma , we have: set theory Z derives for every capital X, open scope, capital X, is transitive implies sigma superscript capital X, close scope . (We used this schema in proposition one in chapter Replacement .) End exercise. This exercise remains unsolved. Exercise. Show that, for every phi belongs to set theory Z , we have set theory Z F derives phi superscript capital V subscript omega plus omega . End exercise. This exercise remains unsolved. Exercise. Confirm the remaining schematic results invoked in the proofs of theorem three in chapter Replacement and proposition one in chapter Replacement . End exercise. This exercise remains unsolved. As remarked in section Replacement and “Absolute Infinity” in chapter Replacement , this shows that Replacement is strictly stronger than theorem five in chapter Ordinals . Or, slightly more strictly: if set theory Z plus “every well-ordering is isomorphic to a unique ordinal” is consistent, then it fails to prove some Replacement-instance. End section. End chapter.

listen_text: Section. Introduction. In chapter Ordinals , we developed a theory of ordinal numbers. We saw in chapter Stages and Ranks that we can think of the ordinals as a spine around which the remainder of the hierarchy is constructed. But that is not the only role for the ordinals. There is also the task of performing ordinal arithmetic. We already gestured at this, back in section The General Idea of an Ordinal in chapter Ordinals , when we spoke of omega , omega plus one and omega plus omega . At the time, we spoke informally; the time has come to spell it out properly. However, we should mention that there is not much philosophy in this chapter; just technical developments, coupled with a (mildly) interesting observation that we can do the same thing in two different ways. End section.

listen_text: Section. Cardinals as Ordinals. In fact, our theory of cardinals will just make (shameless) use of our theory of ordinals. That is: we will just define cardinals as certain specific ordinals. In particular, we will offer the following: Definition. If capital A can be well-ordered, then the cardinality of capital A is the least ordinal gamma such that capital A is equinumerous with gamma . For any ordinal gamma , we say that gamma is a cardinal if and only if gamma equals the cardinality of gamma . End definition. We just used the phrase “ capital A can be well-ordered”. As is almost always the case in mathematics, the modal locution here is just a hand-waving gloss on an existential claim: to say “ capital A can be well-ordered” is just to say “there is a relation which well-orders capital A ”. But there is a snag with definition one in chapter Cardinals . We would like it to be the case that every set has a size, that is, that the cardinality of capital A exists for every capital A . The definition we just gave, though, begins with a conditional: “ If capital A can be well-ordered and so on ”. If there is some set capital A which cannot be well-ordered, then our definition will simply fail to define an object the cardinality of capital A . So, to use definition one in chapter Cardinals , we need a guarantee that every set can be well-ordered. Sadly, though, this guarantee is unavailable in set theory Z F . So, if we want to use definition one in chapter Cardinals , there is no alternative but to add a new axiom, such as: Axiom. Well-Ordering. Every set can be well-ordered. End axiom. We will discuss whether the Well-Ordering Axiom is acceptable in chapter Choice . From now on, though, we will simply help ourselves to it. And, using it, it is quite straightforward to prove that cardinals (as defined in definition one in chapter Cardinals ) exist and behave nicely: Lemma. For every set capital A : List. Next item. the cardinality of capital A exists and is unique; Next item. the cardinality of capital A is equinumerous with capital A ; Next item. the cardinality of capital A is a cardinal, that is, the cardinality of capital A equals the cardinality of the cardinality of capital A ; End list. End lemma. Proof. Fix capital A . By Well-Ordering, there is a well-ordering the ordered pair capital A, then capital R . By theorem five in chapter Ordinals , the ordered pair capital A, then capital R is isomorphic to a unique ordinal, beta . So capital A is equinumerous with beta . By Transfinite Induction, there is a uniquely least ordinal, gamma , such that capital A is equinumerous with gamma . So the cardinality of capital A equals gamma , establishing item 1 of lemma one in chapter Cardinals and item 2 of lemma one in chapter Cardinals . To establish item 3 of lemma one in chapter Cardinals , note that if delta belongs to gamma then delta has smaller cardinality than capital A , by our choice of gamma , so that also delta has smaller cardinality than gamma since equinumerosity is an equivalence relation ( proposition Equinumerosity as an equivalence relation in chapter The Size of Sets ). So gamma equals the cardinality of gamma . End proof. The next result guarantees Cantor's Principle, and more besides. (Note that cardinals inherit their ordering from the ordinals, that is, the cardinal a is less than the cardinal b if and only if the cardinal a belongs to the cardinal b . In formulating this, we will use Fraktur letters for objects we know to be cardinals. This is fairly standard. A common alternative is to use Greek letters, since cardinals are ordinals, but to choose them from the middle of the alphabet, for example: kappa, then lambda .): Lemma. For any sets capital A and capital B : Displayed expression. Source-ordered display. capital A is equinumerous with capital B if and only if the cardinality of capital A equals the cardinality of capital B. Then, capital A has cardinality at most that of capital B if and only if the cardinality of capital A is less than or equal to the cardinality of capital B. Then, capital A has smaller cardinality than capital B if and only if the cardinality of capital A is less than the cardinality of capital B. End display. End displayed expression. End lemma. Proof. We will prove the left-to-right direction of the second claim (the other cases are similar, and left as an exercise). So, consider the following diagram: Commutative comparison diagram. On the top row, capital A maps by an injection to capital B . Vertical bijections connect those two sets, respectively, with the cardinality of capital A and the cardinality of capital B . A dashed bottom arrow is the resulting injection between the two cardinalities. End of diagram. The double-headed arrows indicate bijections, whose existence is guaranteed by the lemma on Cardinals Exist . In assuming that capital A has cardinality at most that of capital B , there is an injection capital A maps to capital B . Now, chasing the arrows around from the cardinality of capital A to capital A to capital B to the cardinality of capital B , we obtain an injection the cardinality of capital A maps to the cardinality of capital B (the dashed arrow). End proof. We can also use the lemma on Cardinals Behave Right to re-prove Schröder—Bernstein. This is the claim that if capital A has cardinality at most that of capital B and capital B has cardinality at most that of capital A then capital A is equinumerous with capital B . We stated this as the theorem on schroder bernstein , but first proved it—with some effort—in section Appendix: Proving Schröder-Bernstein in chapter Infinite Sets . Now consider: Proof. Re-proof of Schröder-Bernstein. If capital A has cardinality at most that of capital B and capital B has cardinality at most that of capital A , then the cardinality of capital A is less than or equal to the cardinality of capital B and the cardinality of capital B is less than or equal to the cardinality of capital A by the lemma on Cardinals Behave Right . So the cardinality of capital A equals the cardinality of capital B and capital A is equinumerous with capital B by Trichotomy and the lemma on Cardinals Behave Right . End proof. Whilst this is a very simple proof, it implicitly relies on both Replacement (to secure theorem five in chapter Ordinals ) and on Well-Ordering (to guarantee the lemma on Cardinals Behave Right ). By contrast, the proof of section Appendix: Proving Schröder-Bernstein in chapter Infinite Sets was much more self-standing (indeed, it can be carried out in set theory Z minus ). End section.

listen_text: Section. set theory Z F C : A Milestone. With the addition of Well-Ordering, we have reached the final theoretical milestone. We now have all the axioms required for set theory Z F C . In detail: Definition. The theory set theory Z F C has these axioms: Extensionality, Union, Pairs, Powersets, Infinity, Foundation, Well-Ordering and all instances of the Separation and Replacement schemes. Otherwise put, set theory Z F C adds Well-Ordering to set theory Z F . End definition. set theory Z F C stands for Zermelo—Fraenkel set theory with Choice. Now this might seem slightly odd, since the axiom we added was called “Well-Ordering”, not “Choice”. But, when we later formulate Choice, it will turn out that Well-Ordering is equivalent (modulo set theory Z F ) to Choice (see theorem in set theory Z F in chapter Choice ). So which to take as our “basic” axiom is a matter of indifference. And the name “ set theory Z F C ” is entirely standard in the literature. End section.

listen_text: Section. Finite, Enumerable, Non-enumerable. Now that we have been introduced to cardinals, it is worth spending a little time talking about different varieties of cardinals; specifically, finite, enumerable, and non-enumerable cardinals. Our first two results entail that the finite cardinals will be exactly the finite ordinals, which we defined as our natural numbers back in definition of the natural numbers and omega in chapter Steps towards set theory Z : Proposition. Let n, then m belongs to omega . Then n equals m if and only if n is equinumerous with m . End proposition. Proof. Left-to-right is trivial. To prove right-to-left, suppose n is equinumerous with m although n is not equal to m . By Trichotomy, either n belongs to m or m belongs to n ; suppose n belongs to m without loss of generality. Then n is a proper subset of m and there is a bijection f colon m maps to n , so that m is Dedekind infinite, contradicting proposition that natural numbers are not Dedekind infinite in chapter Steps towards set theory Z . End proof. Corollary. If n belongs to omega , then n is a cardinal. End corollary. Proof. Immediate. End proof. It also follows that several reasonable notions of what it might mean to describe a cardinal as “finite” or “infinite” coincide: Theorem. For any set capital A , the following are equivalent: List. Next item. the cardinality of capital A does not belong to omega , that is, capital A is not a natural number; Next item. omega is less than or equal to the cardinality of capital A ; Next item. capital A is Dedekind infinite. End list. End theorem. Proof. From lemma five in chapter Ordinal Arithmetic , the lemma on Cardinals Behave Right , and corollary one in chapter Cardinals . End proof. This licenses the following definition of some notions which we used rather informally in part Naïve Set Theory : Definition. We say that capital A is finite if and only if the cardinality of capital A is a natural number, that is, the cardinality of capital A belongs to omega . Otherwise, we say that capital A is infinite. End definition. But note that this definition is presented against the background of set theory Z F C . After all, we needed Well-Ordering to guarantee that every set has a cardinality. And indeed, without Well-Ordering, there can be a set which is neither finite nor Dedekind infinite. We will return to this sort of issue in chapter Choice . For now, we continue to rely upon Well-Ordering. Let us now turn from the finite cardinals to the infinite cardinals. Here are two elementary points: Corollary. omega is the least infinite cardinal. End corollary. Proof. omega is a cardinal, since omega is Dedekind infinite and if omega is equinumerous with n for any n belongs to omega then n would be Dedekind infinite, contradicting proposition that natural numbers are not Dedekind infinite in chapter Steps towards set theory Z . Now omega is the least infinite cardinal by definition. End proof. Corollary. Every infinite cardinal is a limit ordinal. End corollary. Proof. Let alpha be an infinite successor ordinal, so alpha equals beta ordinal plus one for some beta . By proposition one in chapter Cardinals , beta is also infinite, so beta is equinumerous with beta ordinal plus one by lemma five in chapter Ordinal Arithmetic . Now the cardinality of beta equals the cardinality of beta ordinal plus one by the lemma on Cardinals Behave Right , so that alpha is not equal to the cardinality of alpha . End proof. Now, as early as the definition on enumerable , we flagged we can distinguish between enumerable and non-enumerable infinite sets. That definition naturally leads to the following: Proposition. capital A is enumerable if and only if the cardinality of capital A is less than or equal to omega , and capital A is non-enumerable if and only if omega is less than the cardinality of capital A . End proposition. Proof. By Trichotomy, the two claims are equivalent, so it suffices to prove that capital A is enumerable if and only if the cardinality of capital A is less than or equal to omega . For right-to-left: if the cardinality of capital A is less than or equal to omega , then capital A has cardinality at most that of omega by the lemma on Cardinals Behave Right and corollary two in chapter Cardinals . For left-to-right: suppose capital A is enumerable; then by the definition on enumerable there are three possible cases: List. Next item. if capital A equals the empty set , then the cardinality of capital A equals zero belongs to omega , by corollary one in chapter Cardinals and the lemma on Cardinals Behave Right . Next item. if n is equinumerous with capital A , then the cardinality of capital A equals n belongs to omega , by corollary one in chapter Cardinals and the lemma on Cardinals Behave Right . Next item. if omega is equinumerous with capital A , then the cardinality of capital A equals omega , by corollary two in chapter Cardinals . End list. So in all cases, the cardinality of capital A is less than or equal to omega . End proof. Indeed, omega has a special place. Whilst there are many countable ordinals: Corollary. omega is the only enumerable infinite cardinal. End corollary. Proof. Let the cardinal a be an enumerable infinite cardinal. Since the cardinal a is infinite, omega is less than or equal to the cardinal a . Since the cardinal a is an enumerable cardinal, the cardinal a equals the cardinality of the cardinal a is less than or equal to omega . So the cardinal a equals omega by Trichotomy. End proof. Of course, there are infinitely many cardinals. So we might ask: How many cardinals are there? The following results show that we might want to reconsider that question. Proposition. If every member of capital X is a cardinal, then the union of capital X is a cardinal. End proposition. Proof. It is easy to check that the union of capital X is an ordinal. Let alpha belongs to the union of capital X be an ordinal; then alpha belongs to the cardinal b belongs to capital X for some cardinal the cardinal b . Since the cardinal b is a cardinal, alpha has smaller cardinality than the cardinal b . Since the cardinal b is a subset of the union of capital X , we have the cardinal b has cardinality at most that of the union of capital X , and so alpha is not equinumerous with the union of capital X . Generalising, the union of capital X is a cardinal. End proof. Theorem. There is no largest cardinal. End theorem. Proof. For any cardinal the cardinal a , Cantor's Theorem ( the theorem on cantor ) and the lemma on Cardinals Exist entail that the cardinal a is less than the cardinality of the power set of the cardinal a . End proof. Theorem. The set of all cardinals does not exist. End theorem. Proof. For reductio, suppose capital C equals the set of the cardinal a such that the cardinal a is a cardinal . Now the union of capital C is a cardinal by proposition three in chapter Cardinals , so by the lemma on No Largest Cardinal there is a cardinal the cardinal b is greater than the union of capital C . By definition the cardinal b belongs to capital C , so the cardinal b is a subset of the union of capital C , so that the cardinal b is less than or equal to the union of capital C , a contradiction. End proof. You should compare this with both Russell's Paradox and Burali-Forti. End section.

Then, This is very similar to what is now called Hume's Principle , which says:. Then, the Frege number of x capital F of x equals the Frege number of x capital G of x if and only if capital F is equivalent to capital G. End display. End displayed expression. where ` capital F is equivalent to capital G ' abbreviates that there are exactly as many capital F s as capital G s, that is, the capital F s can be put into a bijection with the capital G s, that is: Displayed expression. there exists a relation capital R such that three conditions hold. First, whenever capital R relates v to y, capital F holds of v and capital G holds of y. Second, every v satisfying capital F is related by capital R to exactly one y. Third, every y satisfying capital G is related by capital R to exactly one v. End conditions. End displayed expression. But there is a type-difference between Hume's Principle and Cantor's Principle. In the statement of Cantor's Principle, the variables “ capital A ” and “ capital B ” are first-order terms which stand for sets. In the statement of Hume's Principle, “ capital F ”, “ capital G ” and “ capital R ” are not first-order terms; rather, they are in predicate position. (Maybe they stand for properties.) So we might gloss Hume's Principle in English as: the number of capital F s is the number of capital G s if and only if the capital F s are bijective with the capital G s. This is called Hume's Principle, because Hume once wrote this: Quotation. When two numbers are so combined as that the one has always an unit answering to every unit of the other, we pronounce them equal. (David Hume, one thousand seven hundred forty, part three book one section one) End quotation. And Hume's Principle was brought to contemporary mathematico-logical prominence by Gottlob Frege (one thousand eight hundred eighty four), section sixty three , who quoted this passage from Hume, before (in effect) sketching (what we have called) Hume's Principle. You should note the structural similarity between Hume's Principle and Basic Law V. We formulated this in section Appendix: Frege's Basic Law V in chapter The Iterative Conception as follows: Displayed expression. the Frege extension of x capital F of x equals the Frege extension of x capital G of x, iff, for every x, open scope, capital F of x if and only if capital G of x, close scope. End displayed expression. And, at this point, some commentary and comparison might help. There are two ways to take a principle like Hume's Principle or Basic Law V: predicatively or impredicatively (recall section Predicative and Impredicative in chapter The Iterative Conception ). On the impredicative reading of Basic Law V, for each capital F , the object the Frege extension of x capital F of x falls within the domain of quantification that we used in formulating Basic Law V itself. Similarly, on the impredicative reading of Hume's Principle, for each capital F , the object the Frege number of x capital F of x falls within the domain of quantification that we used in formulating Hume's Principle. By contrast, on the predicative understanding, the objects the Frege extension of x capital F of x and the Frege number of x capital F of x would be entities from some different domain. Now, if we read Basic Law V impredicatively, it leads to inconsistency, via Naïve Comprehension (for the details, see section Appendix: Frege's Basic Law V in chapter The Iterative Conception ). Much like Naïve Comprehension, it can be rendered consistent by reading it predicatively. But it probably will not do everything that we wanted it to. Hume's Principle, however, can consistently be read impredicatively. And, read thus, it is quite powerful. To illustrate: consider the predicate “ x is not equal to x ”, which obviously nothing satisfies. Hume's Principle now yields an object the number of x such that x is not equal to x . We might treat this as the number zero . Now, on the impredicative understanding—but only on the impredicative understanding—this entity zero falls within our original domain of quantification. So we can sensibly apply Hume's Principle with the predicate “ x equals zero ” to obtain an object the number of x such that x equals zero . We might treat this as the number one . Moreover, Hume's Principle entails that zero is not equal to one , since there cannot be a bijection from the non-self-identical objects to the objects identical with zero (there are none of the former, but one of the latter). Now, working impredicatively again, one falls within our original domain of quantification. So we can sensibly apply Hume's Principle with the predicate “ open scope, x equals zero or x equals one, close scope ” to obtain an object the number of x such that x equals zero or x equals one . We might treat this as the number two , and we can show that zero is not equal to two and one is not equal to two and so on. In short, taken impredicatively, Hume's Principle entails that there are infinitely many objects. And this has encouraged neo-Fregean logicists to take Hume's Principle as the foundation for arithmetic. Frege himself, though, did not take Hume's Principle as his foundation for arithmetic. Instead, Frege proved Hume's Principle from an explicit definition: the Frege number of x capital F of x is defined as the extension of the concept capital F is equivalent to capital Phi . In modern terms, we might attempt to render this as the Frege number of x capital F of x equals the set of capital G such that capital F is equivalent to capital G ; but this will pull us back into the problems of Naïve Comprehension. End section. End chapter.

The previous result hints (correctly) that cardinal exponentiation would be quite easy, if infinite cardinals are guaranteed to “play straightforwardly” with powers of two , that is, (by the lemma on Size Powersettwo Exp ) with taking powersets. But we cannot assume that infinite cardinals do play straightforwardly powersets. To start unpacking this, we introduce some nice notation. Definition. Where the cardinal successor of the cardinal a is the least cardinal strictly greater than the cardinal a , we define two infinite sequences: Displayed expression. Source-ordered display. aleph over zero of is defined as omega applied to beth over zero. Then, aleph over alpha ordinal plus one of is defined as the cardinal successor of open scope, aleph over alpha, close scope beth over alpha plus one. Then, aleph over alpha of is defined as the union over beta is less than alpha of aleph over beta of beth over alpha. End display. End displayed expression. End definition. The definition of the cardinal successor of the cardinal a is in order, since the lemma on No Largest Cardinal tells us that, for each cardinal the cardinal a , there is some cardinal greater than the cardinal a , and Transfinite Induction guarantees that there is a least cardinal greater than the cardinal a . The rest of the definition of the cardinal a is provided by transfinite recursion. Cantor introduced this “ aleph ” notation; this is aleph, the first letter in the Hebrew alphabet and the first letter in the Hebrew word for “infinite”. Peirce introduced the “ beth ” notation; this is beth, which is the second letter in the Hebrew alphabet. Footnote. Peirce used this notation in a letter to Cantor of December one thousand nine hundred. Unfortunately, Peirce also gave a bad argument there that beth subscript alpha does not exist for alpha is greater than or equal to omega . End footnote. Now, these notations provide us with infinite cardinals. Proposition. aleph subscript alpha and beth subscript alpha are cardinals, for every ordinal alpha . End proposition. Proof. Both results hold by a simple transfinite induction. aleph subscript zero of equals beth subscript zero is a cardinal by corollary two in chapter Cardinals . Assuming aleph subscript alpha and beth subscript alpha are both cardinals, aleph over alpha plus one and beth over alpha plus one are explicitly defined as cardinals. And the union of a set of cardinals is a cardinal, by proposition three in chapter Cardinals . End proof. Moreover, every infinite cardinal is an aleph : Proposition. If the cardinal a is an infinite cardinal, then the cardinal a equals aleph subscript gamma for some unique gamma . End proposition. Proof. By transfinite induction on cardinals. For induction, suppose that if the cardinal b is less than the cardinal a then the cardinal b equals aleph over gamma subscript the cardinal b . If the cardinal a equals the cardinal successor of the cardinal b for some the cardinal b , then the cardinal a equals the cardinal successor of open scope, aleph over gamma subscript the cardinal b, close scope . If the cardinal a is not the successor of any cardinal, then since cardinals are ordinals the cardinal a equals the union over the cardinal b is less than the cardinal a of the cardinal b , so the cardinal a equals aleph subscript gamma where gamma equals the union over the cardinal b is less than the cardinal a of gamma subscript the cardinal b . End proof. Since every infinite cardinal is an aleph , this prompts us to ask: is every infinite cardinal a beth ? Certainly if that were the case, then the infinite cardinals would “play straightforwardly” with the operation of taking powersets. Indeed, we would have the following: Generalized Continuum Hypothesis (GCH). aleph subscript alpha of equals beth subscript alpha , for all alpha . Moreover, if GCH held, then we could make some considerable simplifications with cardinal exponentiation. In particular, we could show that when the cardinal b is less than the cardinal a , the value of cardinal exponentiation of the cardinal a to the power the cardinal b is trapped by the cardinal a is less than or equal to cardinal exponentiation of the cardinal a to the power the cardinal b . We could then go on to give precise conditions which determine which of the two possibilities obtains (that is, whether the cardinal a equals cardinal exponentiation of the cardinal a to the power the cardinal b or cardinal exponentiation of the cardinal a to the power the cardinal b equals the cardinal successor of the cardinal a ). Footnote. The condition is dictated by cofinality. End footnote. But GCH is a hypothesis, not a theorem. In fact, Kurt Gödel (one thousand nine hundred thirty eight) proved that if set theory Z F C is consistent, then so is set theory Z F C plus GCH . But it later turned out that we can equally add negation GCH to set theory Z F C . Indeed, consider the simplest non-trivial instance of GCH, namely: Continuum Hypothesis (CH). aleph subscript one of equals beth subscript one . Paul J. Cohen (one thousand nine hundred sixty three) proved that if set theory Z F C is consistent then so is set theory Z F C plus not CH . So the Continuum Hypothesis is independent from set theory Z F C . The Continuum Hypothesis is so-called, since “the continuum” is another name for the real line, the real numbers . theorem one in chapter Cardinal Arithmetic tells us that the cardinality of the real numbers equals beth subscript one . So the Continuum Hypothesis states that there is no cardinal between the cardinality of the natural numbers, aleph subscript zero of equals beth subscript zero , and the cardinality of the continuum, beth subscript one . Given the independence of (G)CH from set theory Z F C , what should say about their truth? Well, there is much to say. Indeed, and much fertile recent work in set theory has been directed at investigating these issues. But two very quick points are certainly worth emphasising. First: it does not immediately follow from these formal independence results that either GCH or CH is indeterminate in truth value. After all, maybe we just need to add more axioms, which strike us as natural, and which will settle the question one way or another. Gödel himself suggested that this was the right response. Second: the independence of CH from set theory Z F C is certainly striking, but it is certainly not incredible (in the literal sense). The point is simply that, for all set theory Z F C tells us, moving from cardinals to their successors may involve a less blunt tool than simply taking powersets. With those two observations made, if you want to know more, you will now have to turn to the various philosophers and mathematicians with horses in the race. Footnote. Though you might want to start by reading Michael Potter (two thousand four), section fifteen point six . End footnote. End section.

listen_text: Section. aleph -Fixed Points. In chapter Stages and Ranks , we suggested that Replacement stands in need of justification, because it forces the hierarchy to be rather tall. Having done some cardinal arithmetic, we can give a little illustration of the height of the hierarchy. Evidently zero is less than aleph subscript zero , and one is less than aleph subscript one , and two is less than aleph subscript two and so on and, indeed, the difference in size only gets bigger with every step. So it is tempting to conjecture that kappa is less than aleph subscript kappa for every ordinal kappa . But this conjecture is false, given set theory Z F C . In fact, we can prove that there are aleph -fixed-points, that is, cardinals kappa such that kappa equals aleph subscript kappa . Proposition. There is an aleph -fixed-point. End proposition. Proof. Using recursion, define: Displayed expression. Source-ordered display. kappa subscript zero equals zero. Then, kappa subscript n plus one equals aleph over kappa subscript n. Then, kappa equals the union over n is less than omega of kappa subscript n. End display. End displayed expression. Now kappa is a cardinal by proposition three in chapter Cardinals . But now: Displayed expression. kappa equals the union over n is less than omega of kappa subscript n plus one equals the union over n is less than omega of aleph over kappa subscript n equals the union over alpha is less than kappa of aleph subscript alpha equals aleph subscript kappa. End displayed expression. End proof. Boolos once wrote an article about exactly the aleph -fixed-point we just constructed. After noting the existence of kappa , at the start of his article, he said: Quotation. kappa is. a pretty big number, by the lights of those with no previous exposure to set theory, so big, it seems to me, that it calls into question the truth of any theory, one of whose assertions is the claim that there are at least kappa objects. (George Boolos, two thousand, page two hundred fifty seven) End quotation. And he ultimately concluded his paper by asking: Quotation. do. we suspect that, however it may have been at the beginning of the story, by the time we have come thus far the wheels are spinning and we are no longer listening to a description of anything that is the case? (George Boolos, two thousand, page two hundred sixty eight) End quotation. If we have, indeed, outrun “anything that is the case”, then we must point the finger of blame directly at Replacement. For it is this axiom which allows our proof to work. In which case, one assumes, Boolos would need to revisit the claim he made, a few decades earlier, that Replacement has “no undesirable” consequences (see section Extrinsic Considerations about Replacement in chapter Replacement ). But is the existence of kappa so bad? It might help, here, to consider Russell's Tristram Shandy paradox. Tristram Shandy documents his life in his diary, but it takes him a year to record a single day. With every passing year, Tristram falls further and further behind: after one year, he has recorded only one day, and has lived three hundred sixty four days unrecorded days; after two years, he has only recorded two days, and has lived seven hundred twenty eight unrecorded days; after three years, he has only recorded three days, and lived one thousand ninety two unrecorded days and so on Footnote. Forgetting about leap years. End footnote. Still, if Tristram is immortal, Tristram will manage to record every day, for he will record the n indexed day on the n indexed year of his life. And so, “at the end of time”, Tristram will have a complete diary. Now: why is this so different from the thought that alpha is smaller than aleph subscript alpha —and indeed, increasingly, desperately smaller—up until kappa , at which point, we catch up, and kappa equals aleph subscript kappa ? Setting that aside, and assuming we accept set theory Z F C , let's close with a little more fun concerning fixed-point constructions. The next three results establish, intuitively, that there is a (non-trivial) point at which the hierarchy is as wide as it is tall: Proposition. There is a beth -fixed-point, that is, a kappa such that kappa equals beth subscript kappa . End proposition. Proof. As in proposition eleven in chapter Cardinal Arithmetic , using “ beth ” in place of “ aleph ”. End proof. Proposition. the cardinality of capital V subscript omega plus alpha equals beth over alpha . If omega ordinal times omega is less than or equal to alpha , then the cardinality of capital V subscript alpha equals beth subscript alpha . End proposition. Proof. The first claim holds by a simple transfinite induction. The second claim follows, since if omega ordinal times omega is less than or equal to alpha then omega plus alpha equals alpha . To establish this, we use facts about ordinal arithmetic from chapter Ordinal Arithmetic . First note that omega ordinal times omega equals omega ordinal times open scope, one ordinal plus omega, close scope equals open scope, omega ordinal times one, close scope ordinal plus open scope, omega ordinal times omega, close scope equals omega ordinal plus open scope, omega ordinal times omega, close scope . Now if omega ordinal times omega is less than or equal to alpha , that is, alpha equals open scope, omega ordinal times omega, close scope ordinal plus beta for some beta , then omega ordinal plus alpha equals omega ordinal plus open scope, open scope, omega ordinal times omega, close scope ordinal plus beta, close scope equals open scope, omega ordinal plus open scope, omega ordinal times omega, close scope, close scope ordinal plus beta equals open scope, omega ordinal times omega, close scope ordinal plus beta equals alpha . End proof. Corollary. There is a kappa such that the cardinality of capital V subscript kappa equals kappa . End corollary. Proof. Let kappa be a beth -fixed point, as given by proposition twelve in chapter Cardinal Arithmetic . Clearly omega ordinal times omega is less than kappa . So the cardinality of capital V subscript kappa equals beth subscript kappa by proposition thirteen in chapter Cardinal Arithmetic . End proof. There are as many stages beneath capital V subscript kappa as there are elements of capital V subscript kappa . Intuitively, then, capital V subscript kappa is as wide as it is tall. This is very Tristram-Shandy-esque: we move from one stage to the next by taking powersets, thereby making our hierarchy much bigger with each step. But, “in the end”, that is, at stage kappa , the hierarchy's width catches up with its height. One might ask: How often does the hierarchy's width match its height?
