Evidently zero is less than aleph subscript zero , and one is less than aleph subscript one , and two is less than aleph subscript two and so on and, indeed, the difference in size only gets bigger with every step. So it is tempting to conjecture that kappa is less than aleph subscript kappa for every ordinal kappa . But this conjecture is false, given set theory Z F C . In fact, we can prove that there are aleph -fixed-points, that is, cardinals kappa such that kappa equals aleph subscript kappa . Proposition. There is an aleph -fixed-point. End proposition. Proof. Using recursion, define: Displayed expression. Source-ordered display. kappa subscript zero equals zero. Then, kappa subscript n plus one equals aleph over kappa subscript n. Then, kappa equals the union over n is less than omega of kappa subscript n. End display. End displayed expression. Now kappa is a cardinal by proposition three in chapter Cardinals . But now: Displayed expression. kappa equals the union over n is less than omega of kappa subscript n plus one equals the union over n is less than omega of aleph over kappa subscript n equals the union over alpha is less than kappa of aleph subscript alpha equals aleph subscript kappa. End displayed expression. End proof. Boolos once wrote an article about exactly the aleph -fixed-point we just constructed. After noting the existence of kappa , at the start of his article, he said: Quotation. kappa is. a pretty big number, by the lights of those with no previous exposure to set theory, so big, it seems to me, that it calls into question the truth of any theory, one of whose assertions is the claim that there are at least kappa objects. (George Boolos, two thousand, page two hundred fifty seven) End quotation. And he ultimately concluded his paper by asking: Quotation. do. we suspect that, however it may have been at the beginning of the story, by the time we have come thus far the wheels are spinning and we are no longer listening to a description of anything that is the case? (George Boolos, two thousand, page two hundred sixty eight) End quotation. If we have, indeed, outrun “anything that is the case”, then we must point the finger of blame directly at Replacement. For it is this axiom which allows our proof to work. In which case, one assumes, Boolos would need to revisit the claim he made, a few decades earlier, that Replacement has “no undesirable” consequences (see section Extrinsic Considerations about Replacement in chapter Replacement ). But is the existence of kappa so bad? It might help, here, to consider Russell's Tristram Shandy paradox. Tristram Shandy documents his life in his diary, but it takes him a year to record a single day. With every passing year, Tristram falls further and further behind: after one year, he has recorded only one day, and has lived three hundred sixty four days unrecorded days; after two years, he has only recorded two days, and has lived seven hundred twenty eight unrecorded days; after three years, he has only recorded three days, and lived one thousand ninety two unrecorded days and so on Footnote. Forgetting about leap years. End footnote. Still, if Tristram is immortal, Tristram will manage to record every day, for he will record the n indexed day on the n indexed year of his life. And so, “at the end of time”, Tristram will have a complete diary. Now: why is this so different from the thought that alpha is smaller than aleph subscript alpha —and indeed, increasingly, desperately smaller—up until kappa , at which point, we catch up, and kappa equals aleph subscript kappa ? As in proposition eleven in chapter Cardinal Arithmetic , using “ beth ” in place of “ aleph ”. End proof. Our question for this chapter are: How is the Axiom used, and can it be justified? End section.

We did this, for no other reason than that it is the “industry standard”. Before we discuss any of the philosophical issues surrounding Well-Ordering, then, it is important to be clear that we can depart from the industry standard, and develop a theory of cardinals without assuming Well-Ordering. We can still employ the definitions of capital A is equinumerous with capital B , capital A has cardinality at most that of capital B and capital A has smaller cardinality than capital B , as they appeared in chapter The Size of Sets . We will just need a new notion of cardinal. A naïve thought would be to attempt to define capital A apostrophe s cardinality thus: Displayed expression. the set of x such that capital A is equinumerous with x. End displayed expression. You might want to compare this with Frege's definition of the number determined by x applied to Fx , sketched at the very end of section Appendix: Hume's Principle in chapter Cardinals . And, for reasons we gestured at there, this definition fails. Any singleton set is equinumerous with the set containing the empty set . But new singleton sets are formed at every successor stage of the hierarchy (just consider the singleton of the previous stage). So the set of x such that capital A is equinumerous with x does not exist, since it cannot have a rank. To get around this problem, we use a trick due to Tarski and Scott: Footnote. A reminder: all formulas may have parameters (unless explicitly stated otherwise). End footnote. Definition. Tarski—Scott. For any formula phi of x , let the Tarski Scott set of all x of least possible rank such that phi holds of x, or the empty set if there are none be the set of all x , of least possible rank, such that phi of x (or the empty set , if there are no phi s). End definition. We should check that this definition is legitimate. Working in set theory Z F , theorem three in chapter Stages and Ranks guarantees that the rank of x exists for every x . Now, if there are any entities satisfying phi , then we can let alpha be the least rank such that there exists x is a subset of capital V subscript alpha, phi of x , that is, for every beta in alpha, for every x is a subset of capital V subscript beta, not phi of x . We can then define the Tarski Scott set of all x of least possible rank such that phi holds of x, or the empty set if there are none by Separation as the set of x belongs to capital V subscript alpha plus one such that phi of x . Having justified the Tarski—Scott trick, we can now use it to define a notion of cardinality: Definition. The ts -cardinality of capital A is the T S cardinality of capital A equals the Tarski Scott set of all x of least possible rank that are equinumerous with capital A . End definition. listen_text: Section. The Well-Ordering Problem. Evidently rather a lot hangs on whether we accept Well-Ordering. But the discussion of this principle has tended to focus on an equivalent principle, the Axiom of Choice. So we will now turn our attention to that (and prove the equivalence). In one thousand eight hundred eighty three , Cantor expressed his support for the Axiom of Well-Ordering, calling it “a law of thought which appears to me to be fundamental, rich in its consequences, and particularly remarkable for its general validity” (cited in Michael Potter two thousand four, page two hundred forty three ). But Cantor ultimately became convinced that the “Axiom” was in need of proof. So did the mathematical community. The problem was “solved” by Zermelo in one thousand nine hundred four . To explain his solution, we need some definitions. Definition. A function f is a choice function if and only if f of x belongs to x for all x belongs to the domain of f . We say that f is a choice function for capital A if and only if f is a choice function with the domain of f equals capital A set minus the set containing the empty set . End definition. Intuitively, for every (non-empty) set x belongs to capital A , a choice function for capital A chooses a particular element, f of x , from x . The Axiom of Choice is then: Axiom. Choice. Every set has a choice function. End axiom. Zermelo showed that Choice entails well-ordering, and vice versa: Theorem. in set theory Z F . Well-Ordering and Choice are equivalent. End theorem. Proof. Left-to-right. Let capital A be a set of sets. Then the union of capital A exists by the Axiom of Union, and so by Well-Ordering there is some is less than which well-orders the union of capital A . Now let f of x equals the less than least member of x with respect to the preceding less than ordering . This is a choice function for capital A . Right-to-left. Fix capital A . By Choice, there is a choice function, f , for the power set of capital A set minus the set containing the empty set . Using Transfinite Recursion, define a function: Displayed expression. Source-ordered display. g of zero equals f of capital A. Then, g of alpha. End display is defined by cases. case one, stop!; if, capital A equals the image of alpha under g. case two, f of capital A set minus the image of alpha under g; otherwise. End cases. End displayed expression. The indication to “stop!” is just a shorthand for what would otherwise be a more long-winded definition. That is, when capital A equals the image of alpha under g for the first time, let g of delta equals capital A for all delta is less than or equal to alpha . listen_text: Section. Intrinsic Considerations about Choice. The broader question, then, is whether Well-Ordering, or Choice, or indeed the comparability of all sets as regards their size—it doesn't matter which—can be justified. Here is an attempted intrinsic justification. Back in section The Story in More Detail in chapter Steps towards set theory Z , we introduced several principles about the hierarchy. One of these is worth restating: List. Next item.. Stages accumulate. For any stage capital S , and for any sets which were formed before stage capital S : a set is formed at stage capital S whose members are exactly those sets. Nothing else is formed at stage capital S . End list. In fact, many authors have suggested that the Axiom of Choice can be justified via (something like) this principle. We will briefly provide a gloss on that approach. We will start with a simple little result, which offers yet another equivalent for Choice: Theorem. in set theory Z F . Choice is equivalent to the following principle. If the elements of capital A are disjoint and non-empty, then there is some capital C such that capital C intersected with x is a singleton for every x belongs to capital A . (We call such a capital C a choice set for capital A .) End theorem. The proof of this result is straightforward, and we leave it as an exercise for the reader. Exercise. Prove theorem in set theory Z F in chapter Choice . If you struggle, you can find a proof in Michael Potter (two thousand four), pages two hundred forty two through two hundred forty three . End exercise. This exercise remains unsolved. The essential point is that a choice set for capital A is just the range of a choice function for capital A . So, to justify Choice, we can simply try to justify its equivalent formulation, in terms of the existence of choice sets. And we will now try to do exactly that. Let capital A apostrophe s elements be disjoint and non-empty. By Stages are key (see section The Story in More Detail in chapter Steps towards set theory Z ), capital A is formed at some stage capital S . Note that all the elements of the union of capital A are available before stage capital S . Now, by Stages accumulate, for any sets which were formed before capital S , a set is formed whose members are exactly those sets. Otherwise put: every possible collections of earlier-available sets will exist at capital S . But it is certainly possible to select objects which could be formed into a choice set for capital A ; that is just some very specific subset of the union of capital A . So: some such choice set exists, as required. Well, that's a very quick attempt to offer a justification of Choice on intrinsic grounds. But, to pursue this idea further, you should read Potter's ( two thousand four, section fourteen point eight ) neat development of it. End section.

listen_text: Section. The Banach—Tarski Paradox. We might also attempt to justify Choice, as Boolos attempted to justify Replacement, by appealing to extrinsic considerations (see section Extrinsic Considerations about Replacement in chapter Replacement ). After all, adopting Choice has many desirable consequences: the ability to compare every cardinal; the ability to well-order every set; the ability to treat cardinals as a particular kind of ordinal; etc. Sometimes, however, it is claimed that Choice has undesirable consequences. Mostly, this is due to a result by Stefan Banach and Alfred Tarski (one thousand nine hundred twenty four) . Theorem. Banach—Tarski Paradox (in set theory Z F C ). Any ball can be decomposed into finitely many pieces, which can be reassembled (by rotation and transportation) to form two copies of that ball. End theorem. At first glance, this is a bit amazing. Clearly the two balls have twice the volume of the original ball. But rigid motions—rotation and transportation—do not change volume. So it looks as if Banach—Tarski allows us to magick new matter into existence. It gets worse. Footnote. See Grzegorz Tomkowicz and Stan Wagon (two thousand sixteen), Theorem three point one two . End footnote. Similar reasoning shows that a pea can be cut into finitely many pieces, which can then be reassembled (by rotation and transportation) to form an entity the shape and size of Big Ben. None of this, however, holds in set theory Z F on its own. Footnote. Though Banach—Tarski can be proved with principles which are strictly weaker than Choice; see Grzegorz Tomkowicz and Stan Wagon (two thousand sixteen), three hundred three . End footnote. So we face a decision: reject Choice, or learn to live with the “paradox”. We're going to suggest that we should learn to live with the “paradox”. Indeed, we don't think it's much of a paradox at all. In particular, we don't see why it is any more or less paradoxical than any of the following results: Footnote. text: Section. The Banach—Tarski Paradox. We might also attempt to justify Choice, as Boolos attempted to justify Replacement, by appealing to extrinsic considerations (see section Extrinsic Considerations about Replacement in chapter Replacement ). Let's recap the proof-strategy. We started with some algebraic facts about the group of rotations on the plane. We used this group to partition the unit circle into equivalence classes. We then arrived at a “paradox”, by using Choice to select elements from each class. We use exactly the same strategy to prove Banach—Tarski. The main difference is that the algebraic facts used to prove Banach—Tarski are significantly more complicated than those used to prove Vitali's Paradox. But those algebraic facts have nothing to do with Choice. We will summarise them quickly. To prove Banach—Tarski, we start by establishing an analogue of lemma four in chapter Choice : any free group can be split into four pieces, which intuitively we can “move around” to recover two copies of the whole group. Footnote. The fact that we can use four pieces is due to Raphael Robinson (one thousand nine hundred forty seven) . For a recent proof, see Grzegorz Tomkowicz and Stan Wagon (two thousand sixteen), Theorem five point two . We follow Tom Weston (two thousand three), page three in describing this as “moving” the pieces of the group. End footnote. We then show that we can use two particular rotations around the origin of the real numbers superscript three to generate a free group of rotations, capital F . Footnote. See Grzegorz Tomkowicz and Stan Wagon (two thousand sixteen), Theorem two point one . End footnote. (No Choice yet.) We now regard points on the surface of the sphere as “similar” if and only if one can be obtained from the other by a rotation in capital F . We then use Choice to select exactly one point from each equivalence class of “similar” points. Applying our division of capital F to the surface of the sphere, as in lemma eight in chapter Choice , we split that surface into four pieces, which we can “move around” to obtain two copies of the surface of the sphere. And this establishes (Felix Hausdorff, one thousand nine hundred fourteen) : Theorem. Hausdorff's Paradox (in set theory Z F C ). The surface of any sphere can be decomposed into finitely many pieces, which can be reassembled (by rotation and transportation) to form two disjoint copies of that sphere. End theorem. A couple of further algebraic tricks are needed to obtain the full Banach-Tarski Theorem (which concerns not just the sphere's surface, but its interior too). Frankly, however, this is just icing on the algebraic cake. Hence Weston writes: Quotation. Open bracket. Ellipsis. Close bracket. the result on free groups is the key step in the proof of the Banach-Tarski paradox. From this point of view, the Banach-Tarski paradox is not a statement about the real numbers superscript three so much as it is a statement about the complexity of the group Open bracket. Of translations and rotations in the real numbers superscript three . Close bracket.. Tom Weston (two thousand three), page sixteen End quotation. That is: whether we can offer a finite decomposition (as in Banach—Tarski) or a countably infinite decomposition (as in Vitali's Paradox) comes down to certain group-theoretic facts about working in two-dimension or three-dimensions. Admittedly, this last observation slightly spoils the joke at the end of section The Banach--Tarski Paradox in chapter Choice . Since it is two dimensional, “Banach-Tarski” must be divided into a countable infinity of pieces, if one wants to rearrange those pieces to form “Banach-Tarski Banach-Tarski”. To repair the joke, one must write in three dimensions. We leave this as an exercise for the reader. One final comment. In section The Banach--Tarski Paradox in chapter Choice , we mentioned that the “pieces” of the sphere one obtains cannot be measurable, but must be unpicturable “infinite scatterings”. The same is true of our use of Choice in obtaining lemma eight in chapter Choice . And this is all worth explaining.
